beats.narration_text: This is Onyx, in for Humanitarians AI. This week, fellow Adwait Changan built the Mycroft Finance Investigator — over three weeks, from an empty folder to a local, evidence-driven agent that turns raw financial data into an evidence-backed variance report. The interesting part isn't that it does the math. It's where it stops: it explains the numbers, and hands the why, and the sign-off, to a human.

props.command: Walk me through the Mycroft Finance Investigator you built — the data, the engine, and the agent.
output: Week 1 — a synthetic SaaS ledger: 6 datasets, with schema, provenance, and validation.
Week 2 — a deterministic variance engine: revenue, expense, payroll, EBITDA.
Week 3 — a local agent: selects tools, retains evidence, writes two reports.

beats.narration_text: Act one — the synthetic ledger. Before an engine can find a variance, it needs books to read. Week one built them from scratch.

props.title: The Synthetic Ledger
props.body: Before an engine can find a variance, it needs books to read. Week one built them from scratch.

beats.narration_text: Six datasets, no real company required: budgets, actuals, and the ledger transactions underneath them — plus customers, headcount, and the account mappings that tie a raw transaction to a line on the income statement. Synthetic, but shaped like the real thing.

props.caption: Synthetic SaaS data — shaped like the real thing.

beats.narration_text: What makes it a dataset and not a spreadsheet: every table ships with a schema, a provenance record saying where each number came from, and validation rules. The first run validated forty-three data rows across six synthetic datasets — and a row that fails validation never reaches the engine.

beats.narration_text: Act two — the deterministic engine. Same inputs, same answer, every time. No model guessing in the middle.

props.title: The Deterministic Engine
props.body: Same inputs, same answer, every time. No model guessing in the middle.

beats.narration_text: The engine computes four variances — revenue, expense, payroll, and EBITDA — then does the unglamorous work: it applies materiality rules so a two-dollar gap isn't flagged like a hundred-thousand-dollar one, reconciles control totals so the parts still sum to the whole, and traces every calculated number back to the source records it came from.

props.title: finance.py — ebitda_variance()

beats.narration_text: Here's the headline the sample produced. Budgeted EBITDA: three hundred fifty thousand. Actual EBITDA: two hundred thirty thousand. A gap of a hundred and twenty thousand dollars. The engine's job is to show you that bridge, decomposed — how much came from revenue, how much from expense, how much from payroll — down to the transactions.
Act three — the investigator. Week three wrapped the engine in a local, evidence-driven agent that decides what to look at — and writes down why.

props.title: The Investigator
props.body: A local, evidence-driven agent that decides what to look at — and writes down why.

beats.narration_text: It's a local, evidence-driven agent — no external model in the loop. And it's conditional: it selects finance tools based on what the data shows, not a fixed script. As it works, it retains evidence, records an execution trace of every step, and at the end writes two reports from the same run — one machine-readable for the next system, one human-readable for the reviewer.

props.sparkLine: The agent decides what to look at.

beats.narration_text: The sample run is a receipt you can audit: seven investigation steps, forty-one evidence references retained, twelve tests passed. Every claim in the final report points back to a record. Nothing is asserted that the trace can't support.

props.heading: The sample run
props.body: Seven investigation steps. Forty-one evidence references retained. Twelve tests passed.
props.evidenceNote: Every claim in the report points back to a source record.

beats.narration_text: The verdict. Mycroft is an evidence engine, not an oracle. It validates the books, computes the variances deterministically, and shows its work — the full bridge from budgeted EBITDA to actual, traced to source. What it deliberately does not do is tell you why revenue missed, or sign off on the result. It explains the mathematical performance bridge and leaves business causation and final approval to a human finance reviewer. That boundary is the design, not a limitation. One caveat, stated plainly: this is a synthetic sample and a draft Mycroft workflow — materiality, causal explanations, and distribution still require a named human finance reviewer.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, and think about the boundary before you build: design a deterministic finance-variance engine that traces every calculated number back to a source record, and an agent that retains evidence and writes both a machine and a human report — but never states a business cause it cannot trace. The hard part isn't the math. It's deciding, up front, exactly where the machine should stop.
